segments.english: He said, "Seven ewe-lambs you will take from my hand, in order that they will be to me a witness that I dug this well."
segments.literal: and-said that [object] seven ewe-lambs you-will-take from-my-hand in-order-that she-will-be to-me for-a-witness that I-dug [object] the-well this

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of אָמַר. The verse names no speaker. The answer to Abimelech's question in 21:29 is Abraham's, so he is the speaker.
כִּי after a verb of saying opens the speech. It has no English counterpart here, so the English opens with the quotation mark.
The object marker before the fronted object. The seven ewe-lambs are named before the verb.
שֶׁבַע, the numeral. The pack parses it as feminine. Numerals of this size normally take the opposite gender from the noun, so the form is irregular here; the English is unaffected.
כִּבְשָׂה, a female lamb of the first year. Feminine plural.
Yiqtol, second masculine singular, of לָקַח. The addressee is Abimelech. The form is future in sense, with the force of a request.
מִן with יָד and a first singular suffix: 'from my hand', that is, from me.
בַּעֲבוּר, ב with עֲבוּר, 'on account of'. It introduces a purpose clause, here with a yiqtol.
Yiqtol, third feminine singular, of הָיָה, with a predicate after ל and a person after ל. The subject is the seven ewe-lambs; see grammar.
ל with a first singular suffix: the person for whom the lambs are a witness.
לְעֵדָה: ל with the feminine noun עֵדָה, 'testimony, witness'. Ibn Ezra takes it as the form of עֵדוּת; see commentary.
כִּי introducing the content of the witness: 'that I dug this well'.
Qatal, first common singular, of חָפַר. The act is past, done before the speech.
The object marker before the noun.
בְּאֵר, 'a well', with the article.
זֹאת in apposition to the noun: 'this well'.

phrases.literal: and-said that: the wayyiqtol opens the verse, and the כִּי after the verb opens the speech
[object] seven ewe-lambs: the object stands before its verb

phrases.english: in order that they will be to me

grammar: Abraham's answer to Abimelech's question of 21:29 is one speech, which runs through this verse. The verb in 21:30.1 has no named subject; the context identifies the speaker.

The object, שֶׁבַע כְּבָשֹׂת (21:30.4–5), stands before its verb תִּקַּח (21:30.6), a second masculine singular yiqtol addressed to Abimelech. The English moves the object to the front to keep the Hebrew order.

The purpose clause is בַּעֲבוּר with a yiqtol: 'in order that they will be to me a witness'. The verb is third feminine singular (תִּהְיֶה) although its subject, the lambs, is plural; the form is kept as the pack parses it, and the English 'they' takes the lambs as subject.
The second כִּי (21:30.12) introduces what the witness attests: 'that I dug this well', a qatal of חָפַר. The English keeps the plain claim.
Accents: the zaqef gadol on וַיֹּאמֶר (21:30.1), the etnaḥta on מִיָּדִי (21:30.7) and the silluq on הַזֹּאת (21:30.16) mark the divisions of the verse.
segments.note: The speaker is named by context only, so 'He said' is kept without a name. The lambs are the witness; the English gives no reason for the gift, which the commentators supply (see commentary).

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: לְעֵדָה is like לְעֵדוּת, 'as testimony', the feminine noun for a witness, so the lambs are the witness. He adds a remark on the word for oath, שְׁבוּעָה, which he says he will explain at Numbers 30:3. That remark does not bear on the English.
Rashi's gloss on the purpose clause is the single word 'this' (זאת): the lambs themselves are what is to be a witness. The English agrees.
Rashi reads לְעֵדָה as a feminine form of the noun for testimony, citing 'and the pillar is a witness' (Genesis 31:52). This agrees with Ibn Ezra and with the English 'a witness'.

Rashi tells how the herdsmen of Abimelech quarrelled over the well, each claiming to have dug it, and agreed that whoever was seen at the well with the water rising to meet him owned it. This is the story behind the claim, not the sense of 'that I dug'.
Radak: 'these lambs will be to me' is the thing that I give as a witness. The same reading as the English.
Onkelos renders לְעֵדָה as לְסַהֲדוּ, 'as a witness'. The English agrees.

Sforno compares the act to the shoe handed over in Ruth 4:7 as the sign of an agreement: the lambs are the owners' acknowledgment of the matter. A reader may take the lambs as the owners' acknowledgment rather than a witness; the English keeps the witness.
Sforno glosses בַּעֲבוּר תִּהְיֶה לִּי as 'the covenant' (הַבְּרִית): the purpose is the covenant just made. The English keeps the purpose as the Hebrew states it.
Sforno glosses לְעֵדָה as 'on your acknowledgment' (עַל הוֹדָאָתְךָ), taking the witness to be Abimelech's acknowledgment. The English keeps 'a witness'.

context: The seven ewe-lambs were set apart by Abraham in 21:28, and the text gives only their purpose: a witness. Nothing in the verse says they were a price, a fee or a sacrifice, and the English does not say so.
Scholars compare the giving of animals to mark an agreement over land or water with other ancient agreements. The comparisons are disputed, and the English does not depend on them.

segments.english: Therefore he called that place Beersheba, because there both of them swore.
segments.literal: on-so he-called to-the-place the-that well-of-seven that there they-swore the-two-of-them

tokens.note: עַל כֵּן, 'on so': a compound meaning 'therefore'. It refers back to the lambs and the agreement of 21:30. No sense is taken for עַל.
כֵּן, 'so', completing the compound עַל כֵּן.
Qatal, third masculine singular, of קָרָא. The naming construction is קָרָא with ל and the place, then the name: 'he called the place Beersheba'.
לַ: the ל marks the place as the object of the naming verb. מָקוֹם, 'place, spot'.
הַהוּא: the article on הוּא, 'that', after the noun.
The name בְּאֵר שֶׁבַע, 'well of seven'. The verse gives the reason for the second word in 21:31.8–10.
The second word of the name, שֶׁבַע, 'seven'. It is the root of the verb in 21:31.10.
כִּי, 'because', gives the reason for the name.
שָׁם, 'there', the adverb of place.
Niphal, third common plural, of שָׁבַע: 'they swore', the two parties together. The name's second reading comes from this verb.
שְׁנֵיהֶם: the dual 'two' with a third masculine plural suffix, 'the two of them'. It is the subject of the verb.

phrases.english: because there both of them swore

grammar: עַל כֵּן (21:31.1–2) is the compound 'therefore', 'on so'. It refers back to the seven lambs of 21:30 and begins the explanation of the name.
The naming construction is קָרָא with ל, a place, and then the name: 'he called that place Beersheba'. The English follows the Hebrew order of the phrase.
The name has two words, בְּאֵר and שֶׁבַע. The verse gives the reason for the second, 'because there they swore' (כִּי שָׁם נִשְׁבְּעוּ), which plays on the root שׁבע: 'seven' and 'swear'.
נִשְׁבְּעוּ (21:31.10) is the Niphal, third masculine plural, of שָׁבַע, with the two parties as subject. The dual שְׁנֵיהֶם (21:31.11) is the subject, and the oath is mutual.
Accents: the revia on כֵּן (21:31.2) and the tevir on קָרָא (21:31.3) divide the verse; the etnaḥta on שָׁבַע (21:31.7) divides the name; the silluq on שְׁנֵיהֶם (21:31.11) ends it.
segments.note: The English gives the place name as the text gives it. The meaning of the name is in the grammar notes and the commentary; the English does not explain it.

commentary.summary: Radak takes 'therefore' (על כן) as referring to the seven ewe-lambs. He reads the name as the well's word joined to 'seven' from the lambs, and the naming as a sign of the land's inheritance. A reader may take the name's reason from the lambs; the English keeps the reason the text gives, 'because there they swore'.
Onkelos renders נִשְׁבְּעוּ as 'they confirmed' (קַיָּמוּ) rather than 'swore'. The English 'swore' follows the Niphal sense of שָׁבַע.

context: The name Beersheba is read as 'well of seven' or 'well of the oath'. Both words are in the text: שֶׁבַע, 'seven' (21:28–30), and נִשְׁבְּעוּ, 'they swore', in this verse. The English gives the name only, and the notes give both readings.
Beersheba lies in the northern Negev, at the southern edge of the settled land.

segments.english: So they made a covenant at Beersheba, and Abimelech rose, and Phichol, commander of his army, and they returned to the land of the Philistines.
segments.literal: and-they-cut covenant at-well-of-seven and-rose Abimelech and-Phichol commander-of-his-army and-they-returned to-land-of Philistines

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol, third masculine plural, of כָּרַת. 'Cut a covenant' is the idiom for making one; the English 'made' gives its sense.
בְּרִית, a covenant between men: here the sworn agreement between Abraham and Abimelech.
ב: 'at', the place of the covenant.
The name of 21:31.
Wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of קוּם. Its subject is Abimelech; the singular verb agrees with him, and Phichol is added after it.
The king of Gerar (see 20:2 and 21:22). The lexicon lists several men of this name; this is the first.
פִּיכֹל, the name of Abimelech's commander, with ו 'and'.
שַׂר, 'chief, commander', in the construct with the next word.
צָבָא, 'army, host', with the third masculine singular suffix 'his'.
Wayyiqtol, third masculine plural, of שׁוּב, 'return, go back'. Both men are the subject.
אֶל, 'to', after a verb of motion.
אֶרֶץ in the construct: 'the land of the Philistines', a country or territory.
פְּלִשְׁתִּים, the gentilic: 'Philistines'.

phrases.english: to the land of the Philistines

grammar: Three wayyiqtols carry the narrative: וַיִּכְרְתוּ (making the covenant), וַיָּקׇם (the rising of Abimelech) and וַיָּשֻׁבוּ (the return).
כָּרַת בְּרִית is the idiom 'cut a covenant'. The object is בְּרִית with no object marker. The English 'made a covenant' gives the sense of the idiom.
The singular וַיָּקׇם has Abimelech as subject. וּפִיכֹל, 'and Phichol', is added after it with its appositive שַׂר־צְבָאוֹ, and the plural וַיָּשֻׁבוּ takes both men as subject.
שַׂר־צְבָאוֹ is 'commander of his army': the construct, with a third masculine singular suffix on 'army'.
Accents: the tipḥa on וַיָּשֻׁבוּ (21:32.10) and the silluq on פְּלִשְׁתִּים (21:32.13) end the parts of the verse.
segments.note: The English keeps the plural and singular verbs as the Hebrew has them: one subject is named first, then the second is added. 'So' renders the ו of the first wayyiqtol.

commentary.summary: Ramban takes 'they returned to the land of the Philistines' to mean they returned to their city in that land: Abimelech and Phichol lived in Gerar, which is in Philistine territory, while Abraham lived in Beersheba, also in that land. The English keeps the Hebrew's 'the land'.
Radak has Abraham stay at the well with his flocks a day, two days or longer, and then return to his house in Gerar. This supplies a stay the text does not state.
Onkelos renders the covenant-making with 'they decreed' (גְּזָרוּ) and 'a confirmation' (קְיָם), and the return as 'they returned to the land of the Philistines'. The English keeps 'made a covenant'.

Sforno: they returned from Beersheba, which was not in Philistine territory. They had come there to speak with Abraham, who had gone to look at his flocks, and there Abraham gave sheep, cattle and ewe-lambs to cut the covenant. The English keeps 'returned to the land' as the Hebrew has it.

context: Abimelech is the king of Gerar in these chapters (20:2; 21:22). The title שַׂר צָבָא, 'commander of the army', is a royal military office.

The Philistines: most scholars date the Philistine settlement of the coast to the twelfth century BCE, long after the patriarchs. Whether the name is anachronistic in the patriarchal narratives is disputed; the English keeps the text's name.

segments.english: And he planted a tamarisk tree at Beersheba, and called there on the name of the LORD, El Olam.
segments.literal: and-he-planted tamarisk at-well-of-seven and-he-called there on-name-of the-LORD El Olam

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of נָטַע. The object follows the verb.
אֶשֶׁל. The lexicon gives 'tamarisk tree'. Ibn Ezra gives the word as 'a tree'; Rashi gives 'an orchard' or 'an inn'. See commentary.
ב: 'at', the place of the planting.
The name of 21:31.
Wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of קָרָא. The verb takes בְּ with the name: 'call on the name of the LORD'.
שָׁם, 'there', the adverb of place.
בְּ with שֵׁם in the construct: 'on the name of', the exact designation invoked.
יְהֹוָה, the divine name, rendered 'the LORD' as the decisions set. The pack prints it with the vowels of Adonai.
אֵל, the name of the god: here the epithet's first word.
עוֹלָם, 'eternity, long duration'. The epithet 'El Olam' is transliterated; its meaning is in the notes.

phrases.english: And he planted a tamarisk tree
on the name of the LORD

grammar: וַיִּטַּע is a wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of נָטַע. Its object אֶשֶׁל follows it and carries no object marker.
וַיִּקְרָא־שָׁם continues the narrative. 'Call on the name' (קָרָא בְּשֵׁם) is the phrase used of worship at other patriarchal sites (12:8; 26:25).
The name יְהֹוָה (21:33.8) is rendered 'the LORD' as the decisions set. The epithet אֵל עוֹלָם (21:33.9–10) is two nouns: 'El' and 'eternity' in the construct. It occurs in Genesis only here.
Accents: the qadma on וַיִּקְרָא (21:33.5) and the tipḥa on יְהֹוָה (21:33.8) divide the verse; the silluq on עוֹלָם (21:33.10) ends it.
segments.note: El Olam is the name in apposition to 'the LORD' in the English, as the Hebrew has it. Its meaning (God of eternity, everlasting God) and the commentators' readings are in the commentary and the context notes.

commentary.summary: Ibn Ezra: אֶשֶׁל is a tree (אִילָן), and Abraham planted it as a sign (לְאוֹת). The English 'a tamarisk tree' follows the tree reading; the identification with the tamarisk is the lexicon's. The sign is a reason, so it stays out of the English.

Rashi, quoting Rav and Shmuel, gives two readings of אֶשֶׁל: an orchard that brought fruit to feast the guests, or an inn with every kind of fruit. He also cites the planting of tents (Daniel 11:45). Neither is the tree of the English; a reader may take the word as an orchard or an inn.

Rashi's midrash on וַיִּקְרָא שָׁם: through that tree the name of the Holy One was called God of the world, because guests were told to bless the one whose food they had eaten. This is homily, not the sense of the words.
Radak: Abraham planted near the well so that the tree would witness that the well was his. This is a reason for the planting, not the sense of the words.

Radak takes אֶשֶׁל as a planting word, as in 'under the eshel in Ramah' (1 Samuel 22:6), and as large trees, citing the Talmud's 'great eshalim'. His rabbinic reading of the word as an acronym for food, drink and escort is a midrash and is not the sense.
Radak reads וַיִּקְרָא as 'he gathered the sons there and called to them', in light of the dispute with Abimelech over his wife and the well. The English keeps 'called on the name of the LORD'.

Radak glosses 'on the name of the LORD' as the content of the calling: that people should hold to his faith and serve no other, and by Abimelech's return of the well they would know that he is El Olam.

Ramban takes 'on the name of the LORD' as a proclamation of the LORD who governs time by his strength, and El Olam as the one who rules the whole world. He cites Maimonides (Guide II.13), who took El Olam to point to God's existence before time. Onkelos reads וַיִּקְרָא as prayer. The English keeps 'called'.

Onkelos renders the planting as setting up a tree (נְצֵיב נִצְבָּא), the calling as prayer (וְצַלִּי), and El Olam as 'God of the world' (אֱלָהָא דְעַלְמָא). The English keeps 'called' and the transliteration.

Sforno: Abraham called and made known to the many that God the Exalted is the God of time and its maker, against the view of the new and old Epicureans. He reads the name as the eternal God; the English transliterates the epithet.

context: Tamarisks grow in dry country where there is water near the surface. The planting at a well suits the place; the identification of אֶשֶׁל as a tamarisk is the lexicon's, and the text does not name the species.
El Olam occurs in Genesis only here. The same epithet is used in Isaiah 40:28. The phrase 'call on the name of the LORD' is an act of worship in the patriarchal narratives (12:8; 26:25).

segments.english: And Abraham sojourned in the land of the Philistines many days.
segments.literal: and-sojourned Abraham in-land-of Philistines days many

tokens.note: Wayyiqtol, third masculine singular, of גּוּר: to live as a resident without owning the land. The same root gives the word for a stranger, גֵּר.
The name of the patriarch.
ב with אֶרֶץ in the construct: 'in the land of the Philistines'.
The gentilic, plural.
יָמִים, the plural of יוֹם, 'days'. No preposition marks the duration.
רַבִּים, the plural adjective 'many', agreeing with 'days'.

phrases.english: in the land of the Philistines

grammar: וַיָּגׇר is a wayyiqtol, third masculine singular: the verb opens the clause, and the subject follows it.
יָמִים רַבִּים has no preposition: it is an adverbial phrase of duration, 'many days'. The English keeps it without 'for'.
The adjective רַבִּים agrees with יָמִים in gender and number.
Accents: the darga on וַיָּגׇר (21:34.1) and the silluq on רַבִּים (21:34.6) end the verse. The פ after the verse marks a paragraph division in the Masoretic layout.
segments.note: The verse closes the section about the well and the covenant. The English gives 'many days' without a number, as the Hebrew does.

commentary.summary: Rashi counts the years: Abraham's stay in Hebron was twenty-five years, and here it was twenty-six, so 'many days' exceeds the earlier stay. This is chronology, not the sense of the words.

Radak explains the long stay by the covenant with Abimelech, since Abraham feared no one. He also compares the land of the Philistines with the Shunammite's stay there for seven years of famine (2 Kings 8). This adds a reason and a comparison the text does not give.
Onkelos renders 'many days' as יוֹמִין סַגִּיאִין, 'many days'. The English agrees.

context: The root גּוּר names a dweller who lives in a land without owning it, under the protection of its people. Abraham's stay is not given a number of years in the text.
